GFM's got a [visually-based table format](https://help.github.com/articles/github-flavored-markdown#tables). I'm in two minds about these sorts of things, though. While it makes it easy to construct a table in the first place, they're a nightmare to maintain unless you're au fait with an editor that allows vertical block selection and manipulation (in other words, maintenance becomes something only a coder can easily handle). Still with such an editor, converting the existing tables to this style would be trivial.

As mentioned earlier in this thread, generic markdown has no specific syntax for tables and just defers to inline HTML for tables, so whether you even have the option of using visually constructed tables will depend on what renderer you're using. It wouldn't be too hard to knock together a script to convert the existing tables to HTML, and it might prove easier to maintain for non-coders (although HTML markup is horribly verbose with `<all> <those> <tags>`).

For what it's worth, I don't think any wiki-style markup language has really got this right yet (reStructuredText is even worse - it insists on visual table layout with strict alignment). Or perhaps most text editors are just generally deficient at laying out tables (with the obvious exceptions of vim and emacs).

Yeah we've used GFM's tables before. See [sonic-pi-taster](https://github.com/raspberrypilearning/sonic-pi-taster#music-notes-to-midi-note-values). They work fine on GitHub - and almost work in PHP Parsedown, just seem to break previous list items.

They seem to work happily in Python's [markdown 2 library](https://pypi.python.org/pypi/Markdown):

``` python
>>> import markdown
>>> import urllib2
>>> src = urllib2.urlopen('https://raw.githubusercontent.com/raspberrypilearning/sonic-pi-taster/master/README.md').read()
>>> html = markdown.markdown(src.decode('utf-8'), extensions=['tables']).encode('utf-8')
>>> open('sonic-pi.html', 'wb').write(html)
```

You are the first person outside of the testing team that has submitted a pull request to docs, so you get to be a guinea pig.

When making changes to your own forked repository, it is recommended to commit often (including commits that fix previous mistakes). When presenting this as a pull request, these commits will appear in our version history should we decide to merge them.

For this reason, there should be a concise and logical sequence to the commits in pull requests. In your case, you should have a commit sequence that 
- creates RDP.md with all the changes in one commit
- adds the link in the Readme.md that now references the RDP.md

One commit in your case would be fine, but consider if someone edited Readme.md after you forked the repository: we would end up with a merge conflict. Splitting the changes into two commits would make it more bomb-proof.

`git rebase -i` is your friend. It allows you to rewrite history on your own repository to create a "clean" set of commits for a pull request.

Some explanations are required:

The documentation section of  http://raspberrypi.org is (nearly) automatically generated from the markdown on Github, hosted in raspberrypi/documentation.

The content for the documentation (which is vetted for technical accuracy via the pull request/merge process) is hosted in this repository. Modifications to the _content_ should be made here.

Because of the potential number of people that can comment on or raise issues on the docs tree (and submit needed and useful changes), it makes much more sense to drive a content-driven contribution system.

The preferred method for content contribution is simply to make your changes in a forked repository, then submit an unsolicited pull request. The comment thread on the pull request can adequately contain the discussion for the change proposed, including any subsequent modifications. This obviates the need for the "I think this should be changed" issue / "submit your changes as a pull request" loop.

For items that do not have a documentation alteration, by all means open an issue.

One of the pitfalls of Github is that it does not implement the more complicated git commands. Rebase and merge conflict resolution are among them. You will need to use a command-line interface (or GUI frontend) on a local repository to do this.

If the suggested improvement sounds good, then of course it's even better if the original submitter is able to provide the change themselves.

Be aware there are two types of SDXC cards.

The current generation cards are essentially SDHC with a larger capacity and SD3.0 compatible.
FAT32 will limit you to 32GB for a single partition, but once partitioned with linux fs the whole capacity should be usable.

"real" SDXC cards which are SD4.0 will not work at all since they are electrically different. There is no way of using these on Pi hardware.

Unfortunately whether a card is SD3.0 or SD4.0 is is often not made clear.

Couple of questions on the camera bits: I thought most of the image processing pipeline was indeed GPU based rather than ISP? Obviously I'd defer to James' knowledge on this subject, but I was slightly surprised given it was contrary to what I'd read in some forum posts (from the former firmware devs). The GPU contains the ISP. The ISP is a dedicated chunk of HW inside the VC4 specifically for processing camera images - there are lots of different blocks for different purposes. This HW is controlled from the VPU's which are part of the GPU. They control the passing of the images though all the ISP blocks as they are processed down the 'image pipeline'. In effect, the code running on the VPU's controls all the features of the VC4, camera, 3D, multimedia etc, all of which have their own HW blocks for specific processing. In the camera case, these blocks are collectively known as the ISP. 

There is a suspicion that VS isn't working, which is presumably why that bit has been removed.

I make reference to the B+, as this is the only model that supports high-power devices.

The USB switch is a current-limiting device as this is necessary to prevent dangerous overloads. The current limit is suppressed for 7mS at the commencement of any overload. The action taken by the hub on signalling of current limit by the USB switch is to latch off the power after 20mS of current limit. The 20mS is to act as a de-bounce interval in order to be immune connection of devices that have inrush current.

A message is printed to the kernel message log saying that an overcurrent has been detected. Lack of this message == no overcurrent event.

Ganged power switching is a valid method for switching power to USB ports. It is defined in the USB specification. The 1.2A ganged limit is both intentional and a valid choice. If you want to connect a device (or multiple devices) that exceed this power budget then a powered hub is required.

The hardware undervoltage detection (~4.63V) is tied the PWR LED on the Pi, if this light ever extinguishes or blinks in operation when USB devices are attached to the Pi then all bets are off, as the voltage to downstream devices has gone below the specified minimum.

Connection of high-power devices to model B/A/A+ is possible, and many people in fact use them successfully, but there is an ultimate limit governed by the polyfuse at the 5V input.

Yeah, there's all a big bunch of overlaps, and it can be confusing at first which files get updated by what... ;-)

Going back to the "very start", there's [raspberrypi/linux](https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux) (sourcecode for Pi Linux [kernel](https://www.kernel.org/)) and [raspberrypi/userland](https://github.com/raspberrypi/userland) (sourcecode for Pi [libraries](http://www.raspberrypi.org/open-source-arm-userspace/) and applications - vcgencmd, tvservice, [raspivid](http://www.raspberrypi.org/documentation/raspbian/applications/camera.md), [hello_pi](http://www.raspberrypi.org/documentation/usage/demos/README.md), etc.).
Both of these then get [compiled](http://www.raspberrypi.org/documentation/linux/kernel/building.md), and get added to [raspberrypi/firmware](https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware), along with the binary-only bootcode.bin, start.elf and fixup.dat files ([boot files](https://github.com/raspberrypi/noobs/wiki/Standalone-partitioning-explained#standalone-booting) / low-level firmware).

[raspberrypi/firmware](https://github.com/raspberrypi/firmware) in turn then gets mirrored to [Hexxeh/rpi-firmware](https://github.com/Hexxeh/rpi-firmware) (same files, just in a slightly re-arranged directory hierarchy), and it's this latter repository that is the source of files when you use [rpi-update](https://github.com/Hexxeh/rpi-update). So using `rpi-update` updates the low-level firmware, the kernel (& modules) as well as the Pi-specific libraries (including header files) and applications. And this all exists 'outside' of any package manager and blindly overwrites any pre-existing files - the only way of telling what rpi-update has 'done' is to look at `/boot/.firmware_revision` to see what git-hash from [rpi-firmware](https://github.com/Hexxeh/rpi-firmware/commits/master) you're currently at.

Using `apt-get upgrade` OTOH installs .deb packages from e.g. [archive.raspberrypi.org](http://archive.raspberrypi.org/debian/pool/main/r/raspberrypi-firmware/) which of course _does_ integrate properly with the package manager. And they're also properly split into neat sub-packages (libraspberrypi-bin, libraspberrypi-dev, libraspberrypi-doc, libraspberrypi0 & raspberrypi-bootloader) rather than the all-or-nothing that rpi-update gives you. So I guess at least in _theory_ you ought to `apt-get install --reinstall` **all** of the packages that rpi-update 'tramples over' ;-)

And because rpi-update and apt-get aren't aware of each other, if you run them in the wrong order (e.g. running rpi-update before apt-get upgrade) it's possible for apt-get upgrade to actually overwrite the kernel installed by rpi-update with an older one, but if you try running rpi-update again it will believe that everything is already all up-to-date (until you manually delete /boot/.firmware_revision).

Using rpi-update now includes [DeviceTree](http://www.raspberrypi.org/documentation/configuration/device-tree.md) by [default](http://www.raspberrypi.org/forums/viewtopic.php?f=29&t=97314), whereas apt-get still only 'knows' about the pre-device-tree kernel included in the [Christmas Eve](http://www.raspberrypi.org/merry-christmas-got-a-new-pi/) release of Raspbian. I _suspect_ that the next release of Raspbian (whenever that happens) might also include the DT kernel (at which point it'll be available to apt-get too) but @asb obviously knows more about that than I do.

And as if all that wasn't confusing enough, rpi-update used to be a [manual install](https://github.com/Hexxeh/rpi-update/blob/master/README.md) but it too is now installable from [archive.raspberrypi.org](http://archive.raspberrypi.org/debian/pool/main/r/rpi-update/) ;-)

(And I dare not mention http://nightly.raspberrypi.org/ !! But AFAIK that's (currently?) only used for detecting build-failures, rather than producing 'user installable' packages.)

/sys/class/virtual/gpio/gpio is the wrong location. /sys/class/gpio was there before, and will be there in the future, because it is the right place.

Some things about Linux aren't documented very well, so people make up their own ways to do them. Other things are documented very well (https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/blob/rpi-3.12.y/Documentation/gpio.txt, https://github.com/raspberrypi/linux/blob/rpi-3.18.y/Documentation/gpio/sysfs.txt), but people come up with their own ways of doing things anyway. Switching to using Device Tree has changed some of the implementation details, but the major interfaces - the ones people should have been using - are still the same.

Stuff gets broken with every kernel release - that's why at Raspberry Pi we encourage advanced users before each major update to try "BRANCH=next rpi-update" and make sure it works for them. The "New Device Tree Kernel in testing" thread was started 2 1/2 months ago. You might want to get a preview of the new developments next time, and help us shake out the wrinkles before it hits the mainstream.

Yes, it's supposed to. The purpose of this sequence of commands is to verify that the card has been written correctly. It does so in a rather clumsy way, but it works:

1) Read back the whole card into an image.
2) Truncate that read-back image to the size that was written.
3) Compare the original image with the read back image.

The document says:

> The SD card might be bigger than the original image, and `dd` will make a copy of the whole card. We must therefore truncate the new image to the size of the original image.

dd creates an image of the whole card called `from-sd-card.img`. We then use truncate to discard any of the image that is beyond the size of the Raspbian image. This changes the size of `from-sd-card.img` but not the Raspbian image. Then we use diff to check they are the same.

I agree with @pelwell 
In an ideal world, you'd be able to tell `dd` to only read a specified number of bytes from the SD-card, but unfortunately that's not the way it works, making the `truncate` fudge necessary.

Actually you can, using a combination of "bs" (block size) and "count" number of blocks. You would need to use `stat` to get the size of the Raspbian image, and it might be tricky to choose a suitable block size to be efficient and yet be a factor of the total image size... Ah-ha, the "count_bytes" iflag changes "count" to be in bytes. So it should be possible to say:

```
dd bs=4M if=/dev/sdd of=from-sd-card.img iflag=count_bytes count=`stat -c %s 2016-05-27-raspbian-jessie.img`
```

(although you might want to split it in two for clarity:

The progress will be displayed in the original window and not the window with the `pkill` command; it may not display immediately, due to buffering.

...which could be simplified with something like:

> The `dd` command does not give any information of its progress and so may appear to have frozen; it could take more than five minutes to finish writing to the card. If your card reader has an LED it may blink during the write process. If you want to run `dd` and see the progress, you might want to install the package called `pv` from your default package manager and then use `dd if=raspbian.img bs=4M | pv | sudo dd of=/dev/whatever". That way, you'll be able to see the progress.

Look at it from the point of view of the brand new Raspberry Pi Zero with WiFi user who's never met anything like /boot/config.txt ever before (there's nowt like that that isn't hidden on Windows since we left W95 behind). The parms are daunting. Most of them aren't needed (most of my 14 RPis have three lines in config.txt).  There's some conflicting stuff on the elinux.org wiki as well. We need to be able to point to the RaspberryPi.org pages as say "This is the only reference you need." (plus or minus /boot/overlays/README).

Maybe I've worked with IBM Mainframes too long as they have everying documented as their documentation policy and accept doc changes when you find an undocumented parm or one where code and docs don't match. They'll even take bug fixes if the docs are badly enough broken that they crash your system. It's been like that for 35 years (I used to rip out the Reader's Comment Forms at the back of IBM paper books and mail them in). I even have a special place in the inbox for IBM's IMS Transaction and Database Management system (not /dev/null) with a fast route to their documentation dept.

It becomes a work in progress but doing a review for each change must be a bunch easier than trying to fix something that's got stale. 

BTW, while you're fixing things you should also document which parms set OTP bits/bytes and are sticky after first use (like codec keys and USB/PXE boot). Neat trick doing that - it makes life simpler.

Can you confirm that the HDD is receiving enough power? Does the drive have a dedicated power plug or does it draw from USB?

I haven't attempted to boot from 2.5" HDD, but I can confirm there are significant issues mounting a drive if your raspi isn't getting ~2 amp from USB. The way I understand it, both the pi and drive require about an amp of power each.

Here's a list of what I generally do when I init a raspi:

- `sudo apt-get update/upgrade`
- `sudo apt-get install apt-transport-https`
- Change default username/password
- Ssh-copy-id
- fail2ban
- UFW or Iptables
- Enable ssh and change default port

apt-transport-https will be preinstalled on the next image (if it wasn't already ont he exist one), but it does not add any security. Apt already verifies that package lists are signed and package checksums are correct.

I'd also argue that changing the SSH port does nothing for security. Instead, disabling password logins entirely would be the way to go.

The google-authenticator pam module could be added, but it's probably too much.

A few observations which may or may not be useful:

Unfortunately, there are still bits of Raspbian which have the pi user hard coded in, so some things won't work properly if that user is removed.

There are also bits which require passwordless sudo, which can be considered a security problem worth pointing out.

pkexec provides similar functionality and is also configured to allow the pi user to run commands as root without a password.

Use of visudo can overlook the changes in /etc/sudoers.d/* unless the exact file to edit is passed using the `-f` flag (for example, `sudo visudo -f /etc/sudoers.d/010_pi-nopasswd`)
